title: Transformer architecture
scopeHtml: Self-attention mechanics, normalization, FFN, positional encodings, attention variants (MQA/GQA), KV-cache and FLOPs math, FlashAttention, and why transformers displaced RNNs.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through self-attention for one layer, with tensor shapes. What are Q, K and V, and where do they come from?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Everything else (KV cache, GQA, FlashAttention) assumes you can derive attention with shapes. People who only recite "tokens attend to each other" cannot reason about memory or cost.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "The input is a tensor x of shape [B, T, d]. I project it three times with learned matrices into queries, keys and values. Scores are Q times K-transpose, giving a [T, T] matrix per head. I scale, apply a causal mask, softmax each row, and use those weights to take a weighted sum of V. Each token's output is a mixture of value vectors from the tokens it is allowed to see, then an output projection W_o mixes it back to d."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Let B = batch, T = sequence length, d = model width, h = heads, d_k = d/h.

x            [B, T, d]
Q = x Wq     [B, T, d]  -> reshape [B, h, T, d_k]
K = x Wk     [B, T, d]  -> reshape [B, h, T, d_k]
V = x Wv     [B, T, d]  -> reshape [B, h, T, d_k]
S = Q K^T / sqrt(d_k)     [B, h, T, T]     (one score per token pair, per head)
S = S + mask (-inf above diagonal for decoders)
A = softmax(S, dim=-1)    [B, h, T, T]     (each row sums to 1)
O = A V                   [B, h, T, d_k]
O = concat heads -> [B, T, d]; out = O Wo  [B, T, d]

Intuition: the query is "what am I looking for", the key is "what do I advertise", the value is "what I hand over if selected". Q, K, V come from the same x in self-attention (in cross-attention, Q comes from the decoder and K, V from the encoder). The only place tokens exchange information in a transformer layer is the A V product; the FFN and norms act on each position independently.

Parameters: Wq, Wk, Wv, Wo are each d x d in vanilla MHA, so 4d^2 per layer. Example with d = 4096: 4 x 16.78M = 67.1M parameters per attention block.

Runtime: Q K^T costs about 2 T^2 d FLOPs and A V another 2 T^2 d, so the T x T term is what makes long context expensive. The score matrix is also where memory blows up if you materialize it (see the FlashAttention question).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import torch, math

def attention(x, Wq, Wk, Wv, Wo, h):
    B, T, d = x.shape
    dk = d // h
    q = (x @ Wq).view(B, T, h, dk).transpose(1, 2)   # [B,h,T,dk]
    k = (x @ Wk).view(B, T, h, dk).transpose(1, 2)
    v = (x @ Wv).view(B, T, h, dk).transpose(1, 2)
    s = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) / math.sqrt(dk)      # [B,h,T,T]
    mask = torch.triu(torch.ones(T, T, dtype=torch.bool), 1)
    s = s.masked_fill(mask, float("-inf"))
    a = torch.softmax(s, dim=-1)
    o = (a @ v).transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, T, d)
    return o @ Wo

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying attention "has no parameters": the projections do; the softmax(QK^T)V part has none.
  • Softmax over the wrong axis. It is over keys (last dim), so each query's weights sum to 1.
  • Forgetting that the attention matrix is per head and per sequence, so memory scales with B x h x T^2.
  • Thinking Q, K, V are the raw embeddings. They are learned linear projections of them.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why are Q and K separate matrices rather than one? → The score x_i Wq Wk^T x_j^T is a low-rank bilinear form; separate projections allow asymmetric relations (i attends to j does not imply j attends to i) and let the head dimension be smaller than d.
  2. What is the cost in FLOPs of the score computation? → About 2 T^2 d for QK^T plus 2 T^2 d for AV per layer, so 4 T^2 d total, quadratic in T.
  3. In cross-attention what changes? → Q is computed from decoder states, K and V from encoder outputs; the score matrix is [T_dec, T_enc] and there is no causal mask.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer describes the formula. The senior answer gives shapes, counts parameters (4d^2), identifies the T x T matrix as the memory and compute hotspot, and states that attention is the only token-mixing op in the layer.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Every KV-cache sizing, batch-size and context-length decision in serving comes from these shapes; teams that cannot derive them mis-size GPU memory.

questions.promptHtml: Why do we divide attention scores by sqrt(d_k)? What happens if you do not?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Classic probe of whether you understand the variance argument and softmax saturation, not just the formula.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "If query and key entries have unit variance, their dot product has variance d_k, so its standard deviation grows like sqrt(d_k). Large scores push softmax into a near one-hot regime where gradients vanish. Dividing by sqrt(d_k) restores unit variance so softmax stays in a trainable range."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Assume q_i and k_i are independent with mean 0, variance 1. Then q.k = sum over d_k terms of q_i k_i; each term has mean 0 and variance 1, so the sum has variance d_k and std sqrt(d_k). For d_k = 64 the std is 8; for d_k = 128 it is about 11.3.

Softmax of logits with std 8 is extremely peaked: gaps of 8+ between logits mean the top weight is above 0.999 for most rows. The softmax Jacobian is diag(p) - p p^T, which goes to zero as p approaches one-hot, so gradients to Q and K vanish and the model learns slowly or stalls. Dividing by sqrt(d_k) gives std 1 scores, a soft distribution, healthy gradients.

d_k = 64, raw scores   [ 9.0, 1.0, -3.0, 6.0 ] -> softmax ~ [0.953, 0.0003, 0.000005, 0.047]  (near one-hot)
scaled by 1/8          [1.125, 0.125, -0.375, 0.75] -> softmax ~ [0.43, 0.16, 0.10, 0.30]

The assumption (unit variance, independence) holds at initialization, not necessarily after training; trained models can and do develop large logits. That is why some modern training recipes add QK-norm (normalize Q and K before the dot product) to bound logit growth, which also helps low-precision stability (see the mixed-precision incident question).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import torch
d_k = 64
q = torch.randn(10000, d_k); k = torch.randn(10000, d_k)
raw = (q * k).sum(-1)
print(raw.std())                 # ~8
print((raw / d_k**0.5).std())    # ~1

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying the scale is "to make numbers smaller". The point is the variance of the dot product and softmax saturation.
  • Using sqrt(d_model) instead of sqrt(d_k) in a multi-head implementation.
  • Claiming the scale is a temperature you must tune. It is fixed by the variance argument, though temperature in attention is a real research knob for long-context extension.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What would additive attention do differently? → Bahdanau-style attention uses a small MLP and does not need the scale, but is slower in practice than matmul-based attention; the paper reports dot-product being faster and more space-efficient.
  2. Does the argument hold after training? → Not exactly; it is an initialization argument. Trained logits can grow, hence QK-norm in some recipes.
  3. How does this relate to the fp16 overflow problem? → Large logits can exceed fp16's max of 65504 before softmax; fused kernels compute softmax in fp32 with max-subtraction to avoid it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "to prevent large values." Senior: derives Var = d_k, quantifies the saturation with numbers, mentions the Jacobian vanishing, and ties it to QK-norm and numerical stability.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A reimplementation that scaled by sqrt(d_model) with 32 heads shrank scores 5.7x too much (sqrt(32)), producing blurry, near-uniform attention and a model that trained but plateaued at worse loss.

questions.promptHtml: Why did transformers replace RNNs/LSTMs for language modelling? What did we give up?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you know the real reasons (parallelism, path length, scaling) and the real costs (quadratic attention, KV cache) rather than slogans.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Training. An RNN has to process tokens sequentially, so you cannot parallelize across time and GPUs sit idle. A transformer processes all positions in parallel with matmuls, so it scales on modern hardware. Also any two tokens are one attention hop apart, versus up to n hops through an RNN state. The price is O(n^2) attention compute and a KV cache that grows with context, whereas an RNN has a constant-size state."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
RNN/LSTM            Transformer (self-attention)
sequential ops      O(n)                O(1) per layer
max path length     O(n)                O(1)
per-layer compute   O(n * d^2)          O(n^2 * d + n * d^2)
inference memory    O(d) state          O(n * layers * kv) cache
training parallel   no (across time)    yes (teacher forcing, all positions)

Three reasons it won:

  1. Parallelism. h_t depends on h_{t-1}, so step t cannot start before t-1. Transformers compute every position at once, turning training into large dense matmuls, which GPUs are built for. This let us train on trillions of tokens.
  2. Gradient/information path. Information from token 1 to token n crosses n recurrent steps, with vanishing/exploding gradients and compression into a fixed-size vector. Attention reaches any token directly in one hop, with content-based addressing.
  3. Scaling behavior. Empirically, transformer loss follows smooth power laws with compute and data; this made scaling a reliable bet (see the scaling-laws chunk).

What we gave up: attention cost is quadratic in n, and decoding needs the whole KV cache, so long-context inference is memory-bound. RNNs and modern state-space/linear-attention hybrids keep constant-size state and linear time, which is why they are revisited for long sequences (see the architectures chunk).

Note on RNN inference: autoregressive decoding is sequential for both architectures; the transformer advantage is in training and prefill.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Transformers are better at long-range dependencies" without saying why (path length), or claiming they have unlimited memory. They are limited by context length.
  • Claiming transformers are cheaper. Per token at short context they are not; they are more parallel.
  • Forgetting prefill vs decode: decode is still one token at a time.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does the crossover in compute happen? → Attention cost 4 n^2 d vs FFN/projection cost about 24 n d^2 per layer (for the standard 12 d^2 layer); attention dominates once n is more than a few multiples of d.
  2. Why not just make RNNs bigger/parallel? → Linear recurrences (SSMs, RWKV) can be parallelized with scans; they recover training parallelism but have lower recall on exact retrieval in many comparisons.
  3. Does the transformer have inductive bias for order? → No; permutation-equivariant without positional encoding, which is why we add it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "attention handles long-range dependencies." Senior: parallelism and hardware fit as the decisive factor, path-length argument, the complexity table, and the honest cost (KV cache, O(n^2)).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: The same trade-off shows up as "why is our long-context request slow and memory hungry": the cache that replaced the RNN state.

questions.promptHtml: What is causal masking, how is it implemented, and why can a decoder train on all positions in parallel but must generate one token at a time?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks understanding of teacher forcing, the mask mechanics, and the training/inference asymmetry that everything in serving builds on.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A causal mask sets scores for future positions to minus infinity before softmax so token i only attends to tokens up to i. In training we feed the whole sequence and predict the next token at every position at once, which is valid because the mask prevents leakage. At inference the next token does not exist yet, so we generate one at a time and reuse the KV cache of earlier tokens."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
mask (T=4), 1 = allowed          scores after masking (-inf shown as .)
q0: 1 0 0 0                      s00  .   .   .
q1: 1 1 0 0                      s10 s11  .   .
q2: 1 1 1 0                      s20 s21 s22  .
q3: 1 1 1 1                      s30 s31 s32 s33

Softmax of -inf gives exactly 0 weight. Training: input tokens x_1..x_T, targets x_2..x_{T+1}; one forward pass yields T next-token losses (teacher forcing). Because of the mask, position i's representation cannot depend on tokens after i, so the T predictions are independent training signals computed in parallel.

Inference: the token at position T+1 is sampled from the output at position T and then must be fed back; step k depends on step k-1's sample. Without a KV cache you would recompute K and V for the whole prefix each step (O(T^2) work per token); with it you compute only the new token's Q, K, V and attend to cached K, V.

Padding mask is a different thing: it hides pad tokens in batches. In practice both masks are combined (additive masks added to scores). Encoders (BERT) use no causal mask; decoder-only models always do.

Gotcha: masking with a large negative finite number in fp16 can overflow; a fully masked row with -inf gives NaN from softmax (0/0), which happens with left-padding bugs.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import torch
T = 5
causal = torch.tril(torch.ones(T, T)).bool()
scores = torch.randn(T, T)
scores = scores.masked_fill(~causal, float("-inf"))
print(torch.softmax(scores, -1))   # upper triangle exactly 0

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Multiplying scores by a 0/1 mask instead of setting to -inf: masked positions get score 0, i.e. weight exp(0), and still leak.
  • Thinking the model is autoregressive in training. It is parallel; it is autoregressive in generation.
  • Forgetting the mask applies to prefill in inference as well.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does perplexity look great if the mask is buggy? → The model sees the answer; training loss collapses while generation is garbage.
  2. What is exposure bias? → Training conditions on true prefixes (teacher forcing), inference on the model's own samples.
  3. How do padding and causal masks interact with left-padding in batched generation? → Position ids must be offset for left-padded rows and the pad keys must be masked, otherwise outputs vary with batch composition.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average explains the triangle. Senior ties it to parallel training vs sequential decoding, the KV cache, and the leakage-bug signature (loss too good, generation bad).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A custom training loop shipped with a mask bug that leaked future tokens; train loss fell to near zero within hours, which looked like a breakthrough and was caught only when sampled outputs were nonsense.

questions.promptHtml: Why multi-head attention rather than one big attention? Does it cost more parameters or compute?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many candidates say "different heads learn different things" and stop. Seniors know the cost-neutral split and the actual trade-offs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "I split the d-dimensional model into h heads of size d_k = d/h, run attention independently in each subspace, concatenate, then project with W_o. Parameters and FLOPs are essentially the same as one big head. The benefit is that a single softmax can only produce one weighting per query; with several heads a token can attend to different positions for different reasons, such as syntax, copying or position, in parallel."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Single head with width d: one weighted average per token, so averaging over different relevant positions blurs them together. With h heads each of width d/h you get h different attention patterns. Total cost: projections are d x d regardless of h; the score matmuls cost h x T^2 x d_k x 2 = 2 T^2 d, independent of h. So heads are cost-neutral in FLOPs, though the score memory grows as h x T^2.

d = 4096, h = 32 -> d_k = 128
Wq, Wk, Wv, Wo: 4 x 4096^2 = 67.1M params (same for h = 1 or h = 64)
score tensor per sequence: h x T x T  (32 x 4096 x 4096 x 2 B = 1.07 GB naive fp16 per layer at T=4096)

What heads actually do: interpretability work finds specialized heads (previous-token, induction heads, positional heads) and also many redundant ones; pruning many heads at inference often costs little quality. This is why MQA and GQA (sharing K and V across heads) work: the K/V side is highly redundant.

Choosing h: head dimension 64 to 128 is standard; too small d_k limits what each head can represent and weakens the sqrt(d_k) scale benefits; too few heads reduces pattern diversity. On GPUs, d_k of 64/128 aligns well with tensor-core tile sizes and FlashAttention kernels support specific head dims (verify per kernel version).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Claiming more heads means more parameters. Parameters are fixed by d.
  • Claiming each head is guaranteed to specialize. Many are redundant.
  • Forgetting W_o: concatenation alone does not let heads interact; W_o mixes them.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if h = d (d_k = 1)? → Cost-neutral on paper but each head only compares scalars; quality and kernel efficiency collapse.
  2. How does head count affect KV cache? → Cache scales with number of KV heads, which is why GQA reduces KV heads while keeping query heads.
  3. What can you prune? → Studies show many heads can be removed with small loss, but pruning for speed rarely beats GQA/quantization in production.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "different heads look at different parts." Senior: cost-neutrality argument, h x T^2 score memory, redundancy evidence, and the link to MQA/GQA.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Choosing head count and KV heads when picking or designing a model directly sets KV memory per token and therefore concurrent users per GPU.

questions.promptHtml: What is the residual stream, and what does each transformer block do to it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Shows whether you see the transformer as a stack of read-modify-write operations on a shared vector, which makes depth, norms and interpretability make sense.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Each token has a d-dimensional vector that flows through the whole network. Every attention and FFN sub-layer reads from it, computes an update, and adds the update back. Because of the skip connection the stream is a running sum of all earlier contributions, and gradients flow straight through the identity path, which is what makes deep stacks trainable."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Pre-norm block:

x0 = token_embedding(t) (+ position info if additive)
x_{l+1/2} = x_l + Attn(Norm(x_l))
x_{l+1}   = x_{l+1/2} + FFN(Norm(x_{l+1/2}))
logits    = LM_head(Norm_final(x_L))

So x_L = x_0 + sum of all sub-layer outputs. Consequences:

  • Gradient highway. d x_L / d x_l includes an identity term, so gradients do not vanish through 32 to 80 layers.
  • Shared workspace. Attention heads write information moved from other positions; FFN layers write per-token features; later layers read them. The norm before each sub-layer controls the scale each reads.
  • Interpretability. "Logit lens" decodes intermediate x_l through the output head to see how predictions form across depth; this works precisely because layers write into a common space (imperfectly).
  • Scale growth. The stream norm grows with depth, so output scaling and init matter; that is the motivation for pre-norm and for init schemes like scaling output projections by 1/sqrt(2L) (GPT-2 does this for residual projections).

Intuition for ablations: removing a middle layer in a large model often degrades quality only modestly, because the stream carries most of the information forward and layers make incremental edits.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking each layer replaces the representation. It adds to it.
  • Saying residuals are only about vanishing gradients; they also define the shared communication channel.
  • Mixing up the stream with the KV cache. The cache stores per-layer K/V projections, not the stream.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why do we need a final norm in pre-norm models? → The stream's scale is unbounded; the final norm stabilizes it before the LM head.
  2. What is the cost of a very wide stream? → Parameters scale with d^2 per layer and KV cache with kv_heads x d_k; you trade width vs depth.
  3. Why can early exit or layer skipping partially work? → Layers make incremental edits to a shared space, so intermediate states are already roughly decodable.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "skip connections help gradients." Senior: stream as additive shared workspace, formula x_L = x_0 + sum of updates, pre-norm placement, logit lens, scale growth.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Layer pruning/skipping and activation steering experiments rely on this additive structure; so do quantization sensitivity analyses that find a few "massive activation" dimensions in the stream.

questions.promptHtml: Why does a transformer need positional information, and how do sinusoidal and learned absolute position embeddings differ?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Baseline for the RoPE/ALiBi discussion; checks understanding of permutation equivariance and length generalization.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Self-attention is permutation-equivariant: shuffle the tokens and the outputs shuffle identically, so it has no notion of order. We inject position either by adding a vector per position to the embeddings or by modifying the attention scores. Sinusoidal encodings are a fixed function of position; learned embeddings are a trainable table. Both are absolute and neither extrapolates reliably past the trained length, which is why modern LLMs moved to relative schemes like RoPE."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Without position info, attention treats the sequence as a bag of tokens (plus mask structure for decoders, which leaks a little order but not enough in encoders).

Sinusoidal (original paper): PE(pos, 2i) = sin(pos / 10000^(2i/d)), PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos(...). Each pair of dimensions is a sinusoid at a different frequency, geometrically spaced from wavelength 2 pi to 10000 x 2 pi. For a fixed offset k, PE(pos+k) is a linear function (a rotation) of PE(pos), so relative offsets are in principle easy to learn. No parameters.

Learned: a table of shape [max_len, d]. GPT-2 uses 1024 learned positions (verify for specific checkpoints). Strictly bounded: position max_len + 1 does not exist. Parameters: 1024 x 768 = 0.79M for GPT-2 small.

Sinusoidal Learned absolute
Params 0 max_len x d
Max length Defined for any pos, but attention rarely generalizes Hard limit
Relative info Linear-rotation structure Must be learned
Where added Input embedding Input embedding

Limitations of additive absolute encodings: position info enters once at the input and has to survive through layers via the residual stream; relative distance is only implicit; extrapolation is poor in practice (the original paper found learned and sinusoidal gave nearly identical results and chose sinusoidal for potential extrapolation).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import torch, math
def sinusoidal(T, d):
    pos = torch.arange(T).unsqueeze(1)
    i = torch.arange(0, d, 2)
    div = torch.exp(-math.log(10000.0) * i / d)
    pe = torch.zeros(T, d)
    pe[:, 0::2] = torch.sin(pos * div)
    pe[:, 1::2] = torch.cos(pos * div)
    return pe        # x = tok_emb + pe[:T]

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying sinusoidal "can handle any length" without caveat. It is defined, not reliably used well.
  • Forgetting that without any encoding, an encoder cannot distinguish "dog bites man" from "man bites dog".
  • Adding positions after layer norm or scaling embeddings inconsistently (the original scales token embeddings by sqrt(d_model) before adding).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is relative position preferred now? → Language semantics depend more on distance than absolute index, and relative schemes extrapolate and compose better with caching.
  2. Does a decoder with a causal mask need positions? → It leaks some order via mask structure (a token sees a different number of predecessors), but explicit encoding is still crucial; some NoPE experiments work at small scale.
  3. How would you extend a learned-table model to a longer context? → Interpolate or fine-tune the table; there is no principled extrapolation.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: names both. Senior: permutation equivariance, rotation property, hard limit of learned tables, and why the field moved on.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Fine-tuning older absolute-position checkpoints (GPT-2-style, BERT, many encoders for embeddings) at longer inputs silently fails: 512 is a hard cap, and truncation at 512 tokens quietly drops document tails in embedding pipelines.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between LayerNorm and RMSNorm, and why do most modern LLMs use RMSNorm?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks that you can write the formulas and reason about what is actually removed and why it is acceptable.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "LayerNorm subtracts the mean, divides by the standard deviation, then applies a learned scale and bias. RMSNorm drops the mean subtraction and the bias and divides only by the root mean square, keeping a learned scale. It is cheaper and simpler, and in practice quality is the same, because the re-centering turned out not to matter much while the re-scaling does."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
For a vector x of width d:

LayerNorm(x) = (x - mean(x)) / sqrt(var(x) + eps) * gamma + beta
RMSNorm(x)   = x / sqrt(mean(x^2) + eps) * gamma

Worked example, x = [3, 4], eps ignored: RMS = sqrt((9+16)/2) = sqrt(12.5) = 3.536, output = [0.849, 1.131] times gamma. LayerNorm: mean 3.5, var 0.25, std 0.5, output [-1, 1] times gamma plus beta.

Why RMSNorm: Zhang and Sennrich (2019) argued re-scaling invariance is what helps and re-centering invariance is dispensable. It saves a reduction (the mean), the bias parameters, and some memory traffic; norms are memory-bound ops, so fewer passes matter, though the end-to-end speedup is modest (single-digit percent range in practice; verify per model). Llama-family, Mistral, Qwen and Gemma models use RMSNorm (verify per model card); GPT-2 and BERT use LayerNorm.

Implementation detail that bites: compute the norm in fp32 even when activations are bf16/fp16, then cast back. Llama reference code does exactly this. eps differs by model (1e-5 vs 1e-6), and porting weights with the wrong eps gives small but real logit drift.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import torch, torch.nn as nn

class RMSNorm(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d, eps=1e-6):
        super().__init__()
        self.eps = eps
        self.weight = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(d))
    def forward(self, x):
        xf = x.float()
        xf = xf * torch.rsqrt(xf.pow(2).mean(-1, keepdim=True) + self.eps)
        return (xf.type_as(x)) * self.weight

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Normalizing over the wrong axis (batch instead of feature). LayerNorm/RMSNorm are per token over d, so no batch statistics and no train/eval difference.
  • Confusing with BatchNorm, which depends on batch and is awkward for variable-length sequences.
  • Doing the norm in bf16 and seeing drift versus the reference implementation.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not BatchNorm? → Batch statistics are unstable with variable-length sequences and small per-device batches, and differ between train and inference.
  2. Is RMSNorm faster in wall-clock? → Slightly; fewer ops and parameters, but the norm is a small fraction of step time, so quality parity is the main reason it spread.
  3. What does the learned gamma do? → Per-channel scaling; some channels get very large gamma, linked to "massive activation" dimensions that matter for quantization.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "RMSNorm is a simpler LayerNorm." Senior: both formulas, a worked number, the invariance argument, fp32 accumulation, and eps mismatch when porting.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Weight conversion between frameworks with a wrong eps or bf16 norm shows up as small perplexity regressions that are hard to trace.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between pre-norm and post-norm transformer blocks, and why did LLMs standardize on pre-norm?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests training-stability intuition and whether you know where the norm sits relative to the residual.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Post-norm, as in the original paper, applies the norm after adding the residual: x = Norm(x + Sublayer(x)). Pre-norm applies it to the sub-layer input: x = x + Sublayer(Norm(x)). Pre-norm leaves an unobstructed identity path from input to output, so gradients flow well and deep models train stably without careful warmup. Post-norm can reach slightly better quality when it trains, but it is fragile at depth, so nearly all LLMs use pre-norm."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Post-norm:  x -> [Sublayer] -> (+x) -> Norm -> next      (norm sits on the main path)
Pre-norm:   x -> Norm -> [Sublayer] -> (+x) -> next      (main path is a pure sum)

In post-norm every layer renormalizes the stream, so gradient to early layers passes through L norm operations; analyses (Xiong et al. 2020) show gradient norms near the output are large at initialization, which requires learning-rate warmup and is unstable at depth. In pre-norm the stream is x_0 plus a sum of updates; gradients are well-scaled across layers and warmup is less critical.

Costs of pre-norm: the stream's magnitude grows with depth, so the final layers' contribution to the stream is relatively smaller (a "representation collapse" critique: deeper layers matter less). Hence a final norm before the LM head is mandatory. Variants (DeepNorm, sandwich norms with extra post-norms, QK-norm) exist to recover post-norm quality with pre-norm stability; some recent models add extra norms (verify per model).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
def post_norm_block(x, attn, ffn, n1, n2):
    x = n1(x + attn(x))
    return n2(x + ffn(x))

def pre_norm_block(x, attn, ffn, n1, n2):
    x = x + attn(n1(x))
    return x + ffn(n2(x))

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting the final norm in a pre-norm stack (logits blow up).
  • Using post-norm hyperparameters (high LR, short warmup) with a pre-norm model or vice versa.
  • Claiming post-norm is strictly worse. It can give better final quality at shallow depth; stability is the issue.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What happens to training loss if warmup is removed in post-norm? → Often diverges or stalls early.
  2. Why does pre-norm make deep models easier to extend? → Adding layers adds terms to the sum rather than changing the main path's scaling.
  3. How does this interact with fp16/bf16? → Unbounded stream growth can overflow fp16; bf16 range is safer, and some stacks keep the stream in fp32.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: states where the norm goes. Senior: gradient-path argument, warmup dependence, stream growth, the final-norm requirement, and the DeepNorm/QK-norm family.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Loss spikes in large runs are often mitigated by norm placement and QK-norm choices; teams that copy a config but drop the final norm see immediate divergence.

questions.promptHtml: What does the feed-forward block do in a transformer, and what is SwiGLU? Why is d_ff not 4x d_model in Llama-style models?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: FFNs hold about two thirds of the parameters; interviewers want to see you can count them and explain gated variants.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "The FFN is a per-token two-layer MLP that expands to a wider hidden size and projects back; it is where most parameters and a lot of factual storage live. SwiGLU replaces the single activation with a gated product: SiLU(x W1) times (x W3), then W2. Because it has three matrices instead of two, models shrink the hidden size to roughly 8/3 of d instead of 4 to keep the parameter count equal."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Classic: FFN(x) = W2 act(W1 x), with W1 [d, 4d], W2 [4d, d] -> 8 d^2 params. SwiGLU (Shazeer 2020): FFN(x) = W2 ( SiLU(W1 x) elementwise* (W3 x) ), three matrices [d, d_ff], [d, d_ff], [d_ff, d] -> 3 d d_ff. To match 8 d^2: d_ff = 8d/3, so for d = 4096 the matched value is 10923; Llama-style code rounds up to a hardware-friendly multiple (Llama 3 8B reports d_ff = 14336, which is 3.5 d, because Llama 3 chose a larger multiplier; verify against the model config).

Why gating helps: the second projection acts as a learned, input-dependent gate on each hidden unit, giving more expressive features at equal parameters; Shazeer reported consistent perplexity gains for GLU variants. The reason is empirical.

Role in the network: attention moves information between positions; FFN transforms it per position. Interpretability work frames FFN neurons as key-value memories (keys detect patterns, values write output directions), which is one reason knowledge editing targets mid-layer FFNs. In MoE models, the FFN is the part that is replicated into experts (see the architectures chunk).

Per-layer parameter budget, Llama 3 8B (d = 4096, 8 KV heads, head dim 128, d_ff = 14336):

  • Attention: Wq 16.78M + Wo 16.78M + Wk 4.19M + Wv 4.19M = 41.9M
  • FFN: 3 x 4096 x 14336 = 176.2M So FFN is about 81% of a layer there.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F
class SwiGLU(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d, d_ff):
        super().__init__()
        self.w1 = nn.Linear(d, d_ff, bias=False)
        self.w3 = nn.Linear(d, d_ff, bias=False)
        self.w2 = nn.Linear(d_ff, d, bias=False)
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.w2(F.silu(self.w1(x)) * self.w3(x))

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "SwiGLU is a different activation". It is a gated structure with an extra matrix.
  • Keeping d_ff = 4d with SwiGLU and being surprised the model is 50% bigger in FFN.
  • Forgetting FFN dominates FLOPs at short context.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is SiLU? → x * sigmoid(x), also called swish.
  2. Where is the knowledge stored? → Evidence points to FFN layers acting as key-value memories; attention routes, FFN stores/transforms; this is a model, not a proven decomposition.
  3. How does tensor parallelism split FFN? → W1/W3 column-parallel, W2 row-parallel, so one all-reduce per FFN.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "FFN adds non-linearity." Senior: parameter counts, 8/3 rule, rounding multiples, FFN share of params and FLOPs, key-value memory view.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: When estimating model memory or comparing a "7B" with a "8B" the FFN width explains the difference; wrong d_ff in a hand-written model config silently produces a different parameter count from the checkpoint and loading fails or truncates.

questions.contextHtml:
A teammate wrote a from-scratch causal attention layer for a small 125M-parameter GPT trained on 2B tokens. Training loss drops to 0.15 within 2,000 steps (a healthy run on this data should plateau near 3.0). Sampling from the checkpoint produces repetitive nonsense. Validation loss on a held-out split computed by the same code is also ~0.2. The code:

def attn(x, Wq, Wk, Wv, Wo, n_heads):
    B, T, D = x.shape            # D = 768, n_heads = 12
    dk = D // n_heads            # 64
    q = (x @ Wq).view(B, n_heads, T, dk)
    k = (x @ Wk).view(B, n_heads, T, dk)
    v = (x @ Wv).view(B, n_heads, T, dk)
    s = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) / (D ** 0.5)
    mask = torch.tril(torch.ones(T, T, device=x.device))
    s = s * mask
    a = torch.softmax(s, dim=-2)
    o = (a @ v).view(B, T, D)
    return o @ Wo

Colleagues suggest it is "just a learning-rate issue" and that the tokenizer might be leaking labels.
questions.promptHtml: Find all the bugs, say which one explains the too-good loss, and how you would have caught it before a day of GPU time was wasted.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The scale should be sqrt(dk)" and stops. That is a real bug but it would not produce a loss of 0.15. A weak candidate also blames the learning rate or data leakage without looking at the mask.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the label shift (targets = inputs shifted by 1) tested? Is the same attention function used for validation? Does loss on random-token inputs also go to zero (that would prove a leak rather than memorization)? What are the dtypes?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop the run; the checkpoint is useless. Don't resume it.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Mask applied by multiplication leaks the future. (b) Softmax over the wrong dim. (c) Heads are not formed with a transpose so the view mixes time and head dims. (d) Scale uses D not dk. (e) Label leakage in data (red herring until the mask is ruled out).
  4. How I'd verify each: A causality unit test: perturb token at position j and assert outputs at positions < j are unchanged. Print the attention matrix on T = 4. Run a random-token dataset; loss should stay at ln(vocab). Compare against torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True) on the same weights.
  5. Root cause: s * mask sets future scores to 0, not -inf. After softmax, those positions get weight exp(0)/Z, they are not removed, and since all positions in the row participate, the model can read future tokens, including the answer. Training loss collapses because the target is visible. Softmax over dim=-2 normalizes over queries instead of keys, so rows no longer sum to 1; and view(B, n_heads, T, dk) on a [B, T, D] tensor reinterprets memory so each "head" holds slices from different tokens, scrambling the head structure (no transpose). D ** 0.5 = 27.7 instead of 8 over-shrinks scores 3.5x.
  6. Fix:
q = (x @ Wq).view(B, T, n_heads, dk).transpose(1, 2)
k = (x @ Wk).view(B, T, n_heads, dk).transpose(1, 2)
v = (x @ Wv).view(B, T, n_heads, dk).transpose(1, 2)
s = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) / dk ** 0.5
mask = torch.triu(torch.ones(T, T, dtype=torch.bool, device=x.device), 1)
s = s.masked_fill(mask, float("-inf"))
a = torch.softmax(s, dim=-1)
o = (a @ v).transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, T, D)

Long term: use F.scaled_dot_product_attention(..., is_causal=True) instead of hand-rolling. 7. Prevention: A causality/perturbation test in CI, a shape-assert policy, an overfit-one-batch sanity test, and a rule that a loss far below the dataset entropy floor halts the run. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not tune LR or the tokenizer, and I would not trust "works on a toy" without the perturbation test. Writing attention by hand is fine for learning; production uses fused kernels.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why do the validation numbers also look great? → Validation uses the same leaky attention, so it leaks too; only autoregressive sampling exposes it.
  • After fixing to -inf, you get NaN on a batch. Why? → A fully masked row (left padding with a padding mask) yields softmax(-inf...) = NaN; ensure at least one visible key or use a large negative finite value in the right dtype.
  • Would a bf16 run behave differently? → The leak is logic, not numerics, so no; but -inf vs finite large negatives matter for NaNs.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team trained for two days on an "amazing" run. The tell was a loss below the entropy of the data. The fix took one line; the unit test they added afterwards flags it in 3 seconds.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Mentions only the sqrt scale or blames LR/data.
  • Hire: Finds mask-by-multiplication and softmax dim and explains the leak.
  • Strong hire: Finds all four bugs, proposes the perturbation test and SDPA comparison, and explains why validation did not catch it.

questions.promptHtml: How does Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) work, and why did it become the default in open LLMs?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: RoPE underlies nearly every modern open model and all long-context extension tricks; a fuzzy answer here is a red flag.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "RoPE doesn't add a position vector to the embeddings. It rotates the query and key vectors by an angle proportional to their position, in 2-D pairs of dimensions with different frequencies. The dot product between a rotated query at position m and a rotated key at position n depends only on m minus n, so attention sees relative position directly, with no learned table and no extra parameters."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Split the d_k dims into d_k/2 pairs. For pair i use frequency theta_i = base^(-2i/d_k) (base 10000 in the RoFormer paper; some newer models use a much larger base, e.g. Llama 3 reportedly 500000, verify). At position m, rotate pair i of both q and k by angle m * theta_i:

[q'_2i  ]   [cos(m t)  -sin(m t)] [q_2i  ]
[q'_2i+1] = [sin(m t)   cos(m t)] [q_2i+1]

Rotations preserve the dot product when both are rotated by the same angle, and compose: R(m)^T R(n) = R(n - m). So q_m . k_n = q^T R(n - m) k, a function of relative offset only. Low-index pairs have high frequency (fine local position), high-index pairs have low frequency (coarse, long-range).

Properties:

  • Applied to Q and K only, per layer, not to V and not to the stream. Nothing about position is stored in the KV cache except that K is already rotated (cache stores post-RoPE keys).
  • Zero parameters; norms preserved.
  • Long-range decay emerges from the interaction of many frequencies (RoFormer claims decaying attention with distance).
  • Extrapolation beyond trained length is not free: angles at unseen positions produce out-of-distribution phases for the low-frequency pairs. Position interpolation, NTK-aware scaling and YaRN rescale frequencies; the context-windows chunk covers these.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import torch
def rope(x, base=10000.0):            # x: [B, h, T, dk]; "half-split" convention
    B, h, T, dk = x.shape
    half = dk // 2
    freqs = base ** (-torch.arange(0, half, dtype=torch.float32) / half)
    ang = torch.arange(T)[:, None] * freqs[None, :]      # [T, half]
    cos, sin = ang.cos(), ang.sin()
    x1, x2 = x[..., :half], x[..., half:]
    return torch.cat([x1 * cos - x2 * sin, x1 * sin + x2 * cos], -1)

(Conventions differ: the original RoFormer pairs adjacent dims (2i, 2i+1); Hugging Face Llama pairs dim i with i + dk/2. They are equivalent only if the weights are permuted accordingly; see the RoPE bug scenario.)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Applying RoPE to V or to the embeddings.
  • Applying position to cached keys again at decode (double rotation) or using wrong position ids for the new token.
  • Saying RoPE gives unlimited length. It is relative but trained at a finite range.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why rotate pairs? → A 2-D rotation is the simplest norm-preserving op that composes additively in angle, giving the relative-offset property.
  2. Why does base matter? → Larger base lowers the frequencies, lengthening the wavelengths, which suits longer contexts (the reason newer models raise it).
  3. What do you cache? → Post-rotation keys, plus position index bookkeeping so new tokens use position = current length.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "RoPE encodes relative positions by rotation." Senior: formula, frequency spectrum, what is cached, the pairing-convention gotcha, and why extrapolation still fails.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Context-extension fine-tunes and serving engines all depend on exact RoPE conventions and base; mismatched rope_theta in a config is a classic cause of degraded long-context output.

questions.promptHtml: Compare ALiBi and RoPE. When would you pick one, and what are their length-extrapolation behaviors?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand additive-bias vs multiplicative-rotation position schemes and trade-offs rather than treating RoPE as the only option.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "ALiBi adds a linear penalty proportional to token distance directly to the attention scores, with a fixed head-specific slope; no position vectors at all. RoPE rotates Q and K. ALiBi extrapolates to longer inputs more gracefully out of the box but biases heavily toward recent tokens and has seen less adoption; RoPE gives better quality at trained lengths in most open models and can be extended with scaling methods, so it won."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
ALiBi (Press et al. 2021): score_ij = q_i.k_j / sqrt(d_k) - m_h * (i - j) for j <= i, with slopes m_h geometric, e.g. for 8 heads 1/2, 1/4, ..., 1/256. Heads with large slope attend locally, small slope attends broadly. The penalty is parameter-free and applied at every layer, trained at length L and evaluated at longer lengths with reported perplexity improvements (the paper trains at 1024 and evaluates up to about 2-3x longer, verify exact figures).

RoPE ALiBi
Where applied Rotate Q, K Bias on scores
Parameters none none (fixed slopes)
Extrapolation without tricks Poor Better, modest range
Long-range retrieval Preserved, extendable (YaRN etc.) Built-in recency bias can hurt exact retrieval at far distances
FlashAttention support Easy (pre-rotate Q, K) Needs bias support in kernel (available in FlashAttention-2+; verify)
Used by Llama, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma... BLOOM, MPT (earlier generation)

Takeaway: ALiBi enforces a monotonic distance prior; RoPE leaves the model free to learn non-monotonic patterns (e.g. attend to a header 30k tokens back) because it gives phase relationships instead of a penalty. Post-hoc extension via frequency scaling has proven more flexible than ALiBi's fixed prior, and the ecosystem (checkpoints, kernels, tooling) converged on RoPE.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying ALiBi has learned parameters.
  • Claiming ALiBi "solves" long context. Perplexity extrapolation is not the same as retrieval ability at long range.
  • Mixing up where each applies (bias to scores vs rotating Q/K).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is a linear bias compatible with softmax? → It is a log-space multiplicative decay on attention weights (exp(-m*d)).
  2. What other options exist? → T5 relative bias buckets, NoPE experiments, learned relative biases; the architectures differ in cache compatibility.
  3. Which would you choose for a new 7B model today? → RoPE with an adequately large base, because of tooling, scaling recipes, and benchmarked long-context behavior; ALiBi only with a specific reason.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: lists definitions. Senior: describes the recency-bias trade-off, kernel support, extrapolation vs retrieval distinction, and the ecosystem argument.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: When self-hosting a model with ALiBi (e.g. older MPT checkpoints), engine support for long contexts and kernel bias paths differs from RoPE models; check support before committing to a serving stack.

questions.promptHtml: Explain MHA, MQA and GQA. What do they change, and why does it matter for serving?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The most-asked modern architecture question: it ties architecture to KV-cache memory and throughput.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "In MHA every query head has its own key and value head. MQA shares a single K/V head across all query heads. GQA is the middle: query heads are split into groups and each group shares one K/V head. The KV cache stores keys and values, so cache size per token scales with the number of K/V heads. GQA cuts the cache by h/g, for example 4x with 32 query heads and 8 KV heads, with quality close to MHA."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
MHA : 32 Q heads  32 KV heads   (g = h)
GQA : 32 Q heads   8 KV heads   (4 Q heads share each KV head)
MQA : 32 Q heads   1 KV head    (g = 1)

Computation: query head i uses KV head floor(i / (h / g)). Q projection stays [d, h * d_k]; K and V projections shrink to [d, g * d_k].

KV cache per token = 2 (K and V) x n_layers x n_kv_heads x d_head x bytes per element.

  • Llama-2-7B style MHA (32 layers, 32 KV heads, d_head 128, bf16 = 2 B): 2 x 32 x 32 x 128 x 2 = 524,288 B = 0.5 MiB/token.
  • Llama-3-8B style GQA (32 layers, 8 KV heads, 128): 2 x 32 x 8 x 128 x 2 = 131,072 B = 128 KiB/token.
  • MQA (1 KV head): 16 KiB/token.

Why it matters: decoding is memory-bandwidth-bound; every decode step reads the full KV cache of every sequence in the batch. Fewer KV heads means less memory to hold (more concurrent sequences) and less to read per step (faster per-token latency). MQA (Shazeer 2019) gives the biggest saving but loses quality and training stability; GQA (Ainslie et al. 2023) recovers near-MHA quality, and the paper shows MHA checkpoints can be converted to MQA/GQA with about 5% of original pre-training compute ("uptraining"; mean-pool the K/V heads within each group to initialize).

Tensor parallelism note: with g KV heads and TP degree larger than g, KV heads must be replicated across ranks, so the savings shrink; model choice interacts with deployment topology.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import torch
def gqa(q, k, v):
    # q: [B, h, T, dk]; k, v: [B, g, S, dk]; h % g == 0
    h, g = q.shape[1], k.shape[1]
    k = k.repeat_interleave(h // g, dim=1)
    v = v.repeat_interleave(h // g, dim=1)
    return torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True)

(Production kernels avoid materializing the repeated K/V.)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying GQA reduces compute meaningfully. It mostly reduces memory and bandwidth; attention FLOPs stay the same.
  • Forgetting the cache stores K/V only, not Q.
  • Assuming you can switch a trained MHA model to GQA at load time for free; it needs uptraining.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you convert an MHA checkpoint to GQA? → Mean-pool the K/V head weights per group, then uptrain on ~5% of pre-training compute (per the GQA paper; for MQA conversion).
  2. What is MLA? → Multi-head latent attention (DeepSeek-V2) caches a compressed low-rank latent and reconstructs K/V, shrinking the cache further; verify details per paper.
  3. Does GQA change the number of parameters? → Slightly fewer in K/V projections; models often rebalance FFN width to match.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: definitions and "fewer heads, faster." Senior: gives the exact cache formula with numbers, explains why decode is bandwidth-bound, TP replication interaction, and the uptraining recipe.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Engineers choosing between two "8B" models for a long-context service found 4x difference in concurrent sequences per GPU purely from KV head count; the larger-looking model won on capacity.

questions.contextHtml:
You must self-host a chat model on a single 24 GB GPU (22.4 GiB usable total; budget 90% = 20.1 GiB) for an internal tool. Typical request: 3,500 prompt + 500 output tokens, so plan for 4,096 tokens per sequence. Two bf16 candidates:

  • Model A: Llama-2-7B-style, 6.74B params, 32 layers, 32 KV heads (MHA), head dim 128.
  • Model B: Llama-3-8B-style, 8.03B params, 32 layers, 8 KV heads (GQA), head dim 128. A colleague says "A is smaller, so it will serve more users." Ignore activations and fragmentation for the first pass. Quality is comparable for this task.
questions.promptHtml: How many concurrent 4k sequences does each model fit? Which do you pick and what would change your mind?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "A is smaller so A." It ignores that the cache, not the weights, becomes the binding constraint once weights fit.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Peak concurrency or average? Is the cache dtype negotiable (fp8 KV)? Do requests share a long system prompt (prefix caching)? Latency target? Which engine (paged KV or static)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; the immediate step is to compute, not to guess.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) KV cache dominates capacity after weights. (b) GQA wins on capacity despite more weights. (c) Fragmentation and activations shave 10-20% off both. (d) Quality differences may override capacity.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compute with the formula; then load each in the target engine and read its reported "GPU KV cache size / max concurrency" log line; load test at the intended concurrency.
  5. Root cause (the math):
    • Weights: A = 6.74e9 x 2 B = 13.5 GB = 12.6 GiB. B = 8.03e9 x 2 B = 16.06 GB = 14.96 GiB.
    • KV per token: A = 2 x 32 x 32 x 128 x 2 B = 524,288 B = 0.5 MiB; B = 2 x 32 x 8 x 128 x 2 B = 131,072 B = 0.125 MiB.
    • Per 4,096-token sequence: A = 2.0 GiB; B = 0.5 GiB.
    • Free after weights (20.1 GiB budget): A = 7.5 GiB -> 3 sequences. B = 5.1 GiB -> 10 sequences. So B serves about 3x more concurrent sequences even though it is 19% bigger in weights.
  6. Fix: Choose B. If we still need more headroom: fp8 KV cache (halves cache, accuracy effects must be evaluated; verify engine support), weight quantization to 8-bit or 4-bit (frees weights memory but is a quality trade-off, covered in the serving chunk), limit max context, and enable prefix caching for the shared system prompt.
  7. Prevention: Put a capacity formula into the model-selection checklist: tokens/sequence x KV bytes/token x concurrency + weights < memory x utilization. Track engine KV usage metrics in production.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't choose by parameter count, and I wouldn't ignore the evals: if A scores materially higher on our task the 3 concurrent sequences might be fixed by a bigger GPU. I wouldn't quantize KV without a task eval.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the context is 32k instead of 4k? → B needs 4 GiB per sequence; 5.1 GiB free fits 1; the GPU is too small for this workload without quantization or a bigger card.
  • What if you serve on 2 GPUs with tensor parallel? → Weights and cache are sharded, but with 8 KV heads TP=2 splits 4 per rank; beyond TP=8 KV heads must replicate.
  • Does continuous batching change the math? → It improves utilization of the budget but the budget (sequences x tokens x bytes) is unchanged.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team benchmarked "7B vs 8B" and found the 8B model sustained 3x the sessions on the same card; the surprising part for stakeholders was that the model with fewer parameters was the expensive one.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Chooses by parameter count.
  • Hire: Computes KV per token and concurrency correctly for both.
  • Strong hire: Adds fp8 KV, prefix caching, TP replication, and says to verify with the engine's own capacity log.

questions.contextHtml: An internal assistant serves Llama-3-8B-class bf16 on one H100 (80 GB). Usual prompts are ~1,000 tokens; inter-token latency (ITL) p99 is 25 ms. After a rollout letting users paste whole documents, support reports "the chat freezes for a second". Dashboard: when a 30,000-token request arrives, every other active stream shows an ITL spike to ~1.3 s, then recovers. GPU memory use is 62%, error rate 0%. Someone suggests the KV cache is full. Someone else suggests network problems.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the symptom mechanically and propose the fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Probably memory pressure or network." It doesn't distinguish compute-bound prefill from memory-bound decode and misses head-of-line blocking.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is chunked prefill enabled? Are prefill and decode batched in the same step? What's the max batch tokens setting? Do spikes correlate exactly with long-prompt arrival? Is the cache hit rate relevant?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap prompt length for the interactive tier, or route long prompts to a separate replica pool.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Long prefill monopolizes a scheduler step (head-of-line blocking). (b) KV eviction/preemption (memory is at 62%, so unlikely). (c) Network (spikes align with prompt size, not network metrics). (d) GC or CPU tokenization stall (30k tokens tokenizes in tens of ms).
  4. How I'd verify each: Plot ITL against concurrent prefill tokens per step; read the engine's scheduler logs; test a synthetic 30k prompt on an idle server, which should show a TTFT around the prefill time.
  5. Root cause: Prefill is compute-bound: forward cost about 2 x N x tokens = 2 x 8e9 x 30,000 = 4.8e14 FLOPs; at an effective ~400 TFLOP/s (about 40% of H100 bf16 peak ~989 TFLOP/s; verify) that is ~1.2 s for the weight matmuls alone. Attention over 30k tokens adds a real extra term at this length (roughly doubling the per-token cost), so expect on the order of 2 s or more. If the scheduler runs that whole prefill in one step, all decode streams wait for it. Decode steps normally take ~10-25 ms because they are bandwidth-bound.
  6. Fix: Enable chunked prefill (vLLM's enable_chunked_prefill, with a bounded max_num_batched_tokens, e.g. 2,048), so a 30k prompt is split into ~15 chunks piggybacked on decode steps; ITL spikes become ~100 ms bumps instead of 1.3 s. Longer term: disaggregate prefill and decode onto separate pools; add prefix caching for repeated documents; limit input size by tier. (Serving internals are in the inference chunk.)
  7. Prevention: Alert on ITL p99 by prompt-length bucket; load tests with mixed long/short traffic; SLOs split into TTFT and ITL.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Chunking raises the long request's TTFT somewhat (it shares steps with decode). I wouldn't "add GPUs" first: it multiplies cost without removing the interference.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why isn't decode affected by prompt length? → Decode computes one token per sequence but reads KV; the cost grows with cache size, not with someone else's prefill, unless they share a step.
  • How does TTFT scale with prompt length? → Roughly linear in tokens for FFN/projections plus a quadratic attention term. Attention adds about 4 x L x d x T FLOPs per token = 4 x 32 x 4096 x 30,000 = 1.57e10, versus 2N = 1.6e10, so at 30k it roughly doubles per-token cost (about half that if you count only the causal triangle); verify by profiling.
  • Would a larger model change anything? → Prefill time scales with parameters, so a 70B would freeze for ~10 s on one GPU-equivalent.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "random freezes" ticket was traced to a single user pasting a PDF; the p50 never moved, only p99 ITL, which is why average dashboards looked healthy.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blames network or memory without evidence.
  • Hire: Identifies prefill as compute-bound and decode as memory-bound, proposes chunked prefill.
  • Strong hire: Does the FLOP estimate, discusses disaggregation and SLO split, and verifies with bucketed latency data.

questions.promptHtml: Why is attention O(n^2), and how does FlashAttention make long sequences feasible without approximating attention?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand the GPU memory hierarchy: the bottleneck was IO, not FLOPs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Each of the n queries is scored against n keys, so both compute and the score matrix are O(n^2). Standard attention writes that n by n matrix to GPU high-bandwidth memory and reads it back for softmax and for the V multiply. FlashAttention tiles Q, K and V into blocks that fit in on-chip SRAM, computes softmax incrementally with a running max and sum, and never materializes the full matrix. The result is exact attention with O(n) extra memory and far fewer HBM reads and writes, which gives the speedup."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Naive attention memory: scores per head T x T. For T = 32,768 in fp16 that's 32768^2 x 2 B = 2.15 GB per head per sequence per layer; 32 heads = 68.7 GB for one layer's scores. Infeasible; even if computed layer by layer, bandwidth is wasted.

GPU hierarchy (approximate A100 figures from the paper: ~40 GB HBM at ~1.5 TB/s, ~20 MB SRAM at far higher bandwidth; verify per GPU). Standard attention is memory-bound: write S (n^2), read S, write P (n^2), read P, multiply with V. FlashAttention's loops:

for each block of K,V (size Bc):
   load K_j, V_j into SRAM
   for each block of Q (size Br):
       load Q_i, running (m_i, l_i, O_i)
       S_ij = Q_i K_j^T
       update running max m, rescale previous partial sums, accumulate l and O
       write O_i, m_i, l_i back

Online softmax trick: keep running max m and normalizer l; when a new block has a larger max, rescale the previous accumulator by exp(m_old - m_new). The result equals exact softmax.

Backward: instead of storing P (n^2), recompute S blocks from Q, K and saved statistics (m, l, or logsumexp). That's extra FLOPs but fewer HBM accesses, a net win.

Complexity: FLOPs are still O(n^2 d); extra memory O(n); HBM accesses O(n^2 d^2 / M) where M is SRAM size, which the paper shows is optimal for a range of SRAM sizes. Reported results: about 3x speedup on GPT-2 at sequence 1K and 2.4x on long-range arena at 1K-4K. FlashAttention-2 and -3 improve work partitioning and use newer hardware features (verify specifics).

What it does not do: it doesn't make attention sub-quadratic in compute. At 1M tokens the quadratic FLOPs remain; it only removes the memory wall.

Also relevant at inference: FlashDecoding-style kernels parallelize across the KV length for batch-1 decode, and PagedAttention is a memory-layout idea (cache paging) orthogonal to FlashAttention.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
# One call; PyTorch picks FlashAttention / mem-efficient / math backend
out = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True)
# Force/inspect backend (PyTorch 2.x):
# with torch.nn.attention.sdpa_kernel(torch.nn.attention.SDPBackend.FLASH_ATTENTION): ...

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "FlashAttention approximates attention." It is exact (up to floating-point reordering).
  • "It reduces FLOPs." It doesn't; it reduces memory traffic.
  • Ignoring that fused kernels have dtype, head-dim and mask restrictions; arbitrary masks can fall back to slower paths.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does tiling need online softmax? → Softmax needs the max and sum over a whole row; blocks arrive piecemeal so we maintain running statistics and rescale.
  2. Why is it faster if it recomputes in backward? → Memory-bound ops dominate; recompute is cheap relative to HBM transfers.
  3. Does it help decode? → Less for single-token queries, where the issue is reading the KV cache; specialized split-KV decode kernels help.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "memory-efficient attention, faster." Senior: HBM vs SRAM, online softmax mechanics, exactness, unchanged FLOPs, backward recomputation, and the limits.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Enabling a fused attention backend often turns an OOM at 16k context into a working run; mismatched mask types silently falling back to the math path is a common perf regression.

questions.contextHtml: Your service runs a 70B-class model (80 layers, 8 KV heads, head dim 128, bf16 weights = 140 GB, bf16 KV cache). Today: 2 requests/s, average request holds 6,000 tokens of context (5,500 prompt + 500 output) and lives for 15 s (Little's law gives ~30 concurrent sequences). One replica on 4 x H100 80 GB (tensor parallel 4) is fine. Marketing expects 10x traffic in six weeks: 20 req/s, same shape. Finance asks "how many GPUs?" and the platform lead proposes "just 10x it: 40 GPUs".
questions.promptHtml: Estimate GPUs required and say which levers reduce it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "10x traffic means 10x GPUs." It ignores that current replica is under-utilized or that memory, not compute, is the binding constraint, and gives no numbers.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the 15 s mostly decode time? What are TTFT/ITL SLOs? Is there a shared system prompt (prefix cache)? Can we use fp8 weights or KV? What's the traffic shape (peak vs average)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed now; this is capacity planning. Put the load shedding policy and per-user limits in place before launch.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Concurrency (and thus KV memory) is the sizing driver, not QPS. (b) Per-replica capacity is bounded by free HBM after weights. (c) Compute/bandwidth for decode may become the next limit. (d) Prefix caching could cut prefill.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compute with the formula; benchmark one replica with a realistic trace to find the saturation concurrency; compare with the engine's KV capacity log.
  5. Root cause (the math):
    • KV per token = 2 x 80 x 8 x 128 x 2 B = 327,680 B = 320 KiB.
    • Per sequence at 6,000 tokens: 6000 x 320 KiB = 1.83 GiB.
    • Target concurrency = 20 req/s x 15 s = 300 sequences -> 300 x 1.83 = 549 GiB of KV.
    • Per replica (TP4 = 320 GB raw, ~0.9 utilization = 288 GB; minus 140 GB weights; minus ~10% overhead) leaves ~130-140 GB, about 70-75 sequences.
    • 300 / 72 = ~4.2 -> 5 replicas = 20 GPUs, before headroom for peaks (+30%: ~6 replicas = 24 GPUs). Today's 1 replica holds 30 sequences, i.e. 40% utilized, so 10x traffic needs ~4-6x GPUs, not 10x.
  6. Fix / plan: Fp8 weights (140 -> 70 GB) frees roughly 70 GB per replica and roughly doubles sequences per replica; fp8 KV halves cache per sequence (both require task evals; verify engine support). Prefix caching on the 1,500-token system prompt, if one exists. Autoscale on KV utilization, not CPU.
  7. Prevention: Dashboards: KV cache usage %, preemption count, queue depth, running sequences. Load tests at 1.5x forecast. Reserve capacity for failure of one replica (N+1).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't size on QPS alone and I wouldn't quantize both weights and KV at once without quality evals; I wouldn't skip N+1.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Decode becomes bandwidth-bound: is memory the only limit? → Each step reads weights (140 GB / TP shards) plus all KV; at 72 sequences KV reads (132 GB) are comparable to weights, so latency grows with concurrency; check ITL SLO at saturation.
  • What if avg context doubled to 12k? → Sequences per replica halve (~36), replicas double.
  • What if you switch to an MHA model? → KV per token x8 (64 heads vs 8 assumed MHA equivalent), a replica would hold ~9 sequences: the plan collapses.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A launch plan priced GPUs from QPS and benchmarked tokens/s; the real limit was KV capacity at the p95 context length, found in staging by raising context from 4k to 8k and watching preemptions climb.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Linear scaling by QPS.
  • Hire: Little's law plus KV per sequence math, per-replica capacity.
  • Strong hire: Adds N+1, fp8, prefix cache, bandwidth check, and verifies by load test.

questions.promptHtml: Derive the parameter count of a decoder-only transformer from its config. How do you check "8B" for a Llama-3-8B-style model?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Quick mental modelling of memory and cost; separates people who can size models from those who read marketing numbers.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Per layer: attention projections plus FFN plus norms, times layers, plus embeddings (and the LM head if untied). For d = 4096, 32 layers, 8 KV heads of dim 128, SwiGLU with d_ff = 14336 and a 128,256-token vocabulary: about 218M per layer, 6.98B for layers, plus 525M for embeddings and 525M for the untied head, which sums to about 8.03B."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
General formulas (no biases, SwiGLU, GQA):

  • Attention per layer: d x (h d_k) [Q] + 2 x d x (g d_k) [K, V] + (h d_k) x d [O].
  • FFN per layer: 3 x d x d_ff.
  • Norms: 2 x d per layer (negligible), plus a final norm.
  • Embedding: V x d. LM head: V x d unless tied.

Llama-3-8B-style check (d = 4096, L = 32, h = 32, g = 8, d_k = 128, d_ff = 14336, V = 128,256):

  • Q: 4096 x 4096 = 16.78M; O: 16.78M; K: 4096 x 1024 = 4.19M; V: 4.19M -> attention 41.94M.
  • FFN: 3 x 4096 x 14336 = 176.16M.
  • Layer = 218.1M; x 32 = 6.98B.
  • Embedding 128,256 x 4096 = 525.3M; untied head 525.3M.
  • Total = 6.98 + 1.05 = 8.03B. Matches the advertised ~8B (verify against the model config).

Rule of thumb for the classical (MHA, d_ff = 4d or SwiGLU 8d/3): params per layer ~ 12 d^2; so N ~ 12 L d^2 + V d. GPT-3 175B check: 12 x 96 x 12288^2 = 174B.

Memory implications: bf16 weights = 2 B x N (8.03B -> 16.06 GB). Training with Adam in mixed precision needs about 16 bytes per parameter (bf16 weights + fp32 master + two fp32 moments + grads; exact accounting depends on the recipe, verify) -> 128 GB for 8B before activations, hence sharding (ZeRO/FSDP).

Embedding share matters for small models: for a 1B model with V = 128k and d = 2048, embedding is 262M, 21% of total. That's why tying input/output embeddings is common in small models.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
def params(d, L, h, g, dk, dff, V, tied=False):
    attn = d*h*dk + 2*d*g*dk + h*dk*d
    ffn = 3*d*dff
    layer = attn + ffn + 2*d
    emb = V*d
    return L*layer + emb + (0 if tied else emb) + d

print(params(4096, 32, 32, 8, 128, 14336, 128256) / 1e9)   # ~8.03

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting embeddings, which are big with 128k vocabularies.
  • Counting full K/V projections in a GQA model.
  • Using 4d for d_ff with SwiGLU.
  • Equating parameters with memory when serving: KV cache and activations are extra.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What's the training memory per parameter? → ~16 B with Adam mixed precision (2 weights + 4 master + 4 + 4 moments + 2 grads), varies by recipe.
  2. How would MoE change the count? → FFN replicated per expert; total parameters rise while active per token stay small (see the architectures chunk).
  3. Why 128k vocab hurts small models? → Embedding/head share of parameters and the logits tensor (see the LM head scenario).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "~12 L d^2." Senior: exact formula with GQA and SwiGLU, validation against a real config, and memory consequences for training and serving.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Hand-written configs with a wrong d_ff or KV head count are caught instantly by comparing the computed count with the checkpoint's tensor shapes before a long download or conversion.

questions.promptHtml: Estimate the FLOPs to train and to run inference on a transformer. Where do 6ND and 2N come from, and where does the formula break?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Budgeting GPUs and time requires this fluently; it's a classic whiteboard question.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Every parameter participates in one multiply and one add per token in the forward pass, so inference costs about 2N FLOPs per token. Backward costs about twice the forward, so training is about 6N per token, or 6ND for D tokens. This ignores the attention score terms, which add roughly 4 x L x d x T per token and matter at long context, and it ignores the real-world efficiency gap, usually 30-50% of peak."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A matmul of [T, a] by [a, b] costs 2Tab FLOPs. Summing over all weight matrices, forward = 2 x (params in matmuls) x tokens. Backward needs gradients w.r.t. activations (another 2) and weights (another 2), so total 6 per parameter per token. Embedding lookups are not matmuls, so use N excluding the input embedding (but including the LM head).

Attention extra (per token, forward): QK^T = 2 x T x d_model, AV = 2 x T x d_model per layer -> 4 x L x d x T (T = context length; use T/2 average for causal masks if you count only needed entries). Llama-3-8B-style at T = 8,192: 4 x 32 x 4096 x 8192 = 4.3 GFLOPs vs 2N = 16 GFLOPs, so 27% extra at 8k (and 13% if causal-halved). At T = 128k it's several times 2N.

Worked training budget: 8B params, 15T tokens: 6 x 8e9 x 15e12 = 7.2e23 FLOPs. H100 bf16 dense peak ~989 TFLOP/s; at 40% MFU = ~400 TFLOP/s -> 7.2e23 / 4e14 = 1.8e9 GPU-seconds = 500k GPU-hours. Published training reports for comparable models cite higher GPU-hours (e.g. around 1.3M H100-hours for an 8B-class model; verify) because of lower MFU, restarts and extra overhead, so treat the formula as a lower bound.

Activation recomputation (checkpointing) adds ~1 extra forward: 8N instead of 6N for hardware FLOPs.

Inference: decode is not FLOP-bound. 2N = 16 GFLOPs per token vs the bandwidth needed to read 16 GB of weights; the GPU does ~1 FLOP per byte at batch 1 versus a ridge point near 300 FLOPs/byte (see the decode scenario).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
def train_flops(n_params, tokens): return 6 * n_params * tokens
def gpu_hours(flops, peak=989e12, mfu=0.4): return flops / (peak*mfu) / 3600
print(gpu_hours(train_flops(8e9, 15e12)))   # ~500k

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Counting embeddings or using total (not active) params for MoE.
  • Ignoring MFU and stating peak throughput as achieved.
  • Using 6ND for inference.
  • Forgetting attention terms at long context.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is MFU? → Model FLOPs utilization: achieved model FLOPs per second over hardware peak; 30-55% is typical for well-tuned large runs (verify).
  2. Why backward is 2x forward? → One matmul for input grads, one for weight grads.
  3. How do you adjust for MoE? → Use active parameters per token for FLOPs; total for memory.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: quotes 6ND. Senior: derives it, includes attention and recompute terms, applies MFU, and explains why it's a lower bound.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Training-run quotes from vendors differ 2-3x; this formula plus a stated MFU is how you sanity-check them.

questions.contextHtml: A product lead says: "We need a small model trained on our data. Can we do it in two weeks? How many GPUs?" Details trickle in: the domain corpus is ~100B tokens after dedup; they want a 1B-parameter model; budget is whatever H100s (80 GB, ~$2.50/GPU-hour assumed; verify actual pricing) the cloud team can spare. Nobody has said whether to train from scratch or continue from an open checkpoint, nor what quality means.
questions.promptHtml: What do you ask and what is your estimate for from-scratch training?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Guesses "8 GPUs" with no math, or starts a from-scratch run without discussing whether continued pretraining or fine-tuning suffices.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Why from scratch, and is continued pretraining or SFT of an open model acceptable (cheaper, usually better)? What task metric defines success? Is 100B tokens unique or repeated epochs? License/data restrictions? Inference target hardware (decides size)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; I'd write down the assumptions and a calculation before anyone commits GPUs.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) A from-scratch 1B on 100B tokens is feasible compute-wise but will underperform a continued-pretrained open 1B-8B model trained on trillions of tokens. (b) Data quality and eval matter more than raw compute. (c) The real constraint is engineering (data pipeline, checkpointing), not FLOPs.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compute budget; check a baseline open model on the target eval; run a small pilot (100M model, 2B tokens) to get throughput and MFU.
  5. Root cause (the math): FLOPs = 6 x N x D = 6 x 1e9 x 1e11 = 6e20. At 40% MFU of 989 TFLOP/s = 396 TFLOP/s -> 6e20 / 3.96e14 = 1.5e6 GPU-seconds = 421 GPU-hours. In a 14-day window (336 h) that's about 1.3 GPUs in theory, so 8 GPUs finish in ~53 hours at the same MFU; at a realistic 25% MFU for a small model plus restarts, about 100 hours on 8 GPUs, roughly 4 days, cost ~ 800 GPU-hours x $2.5 = $2,000. Compute is not the obstacle. Compare: Chinchilla-style compute-optimal tokens for 1B are roughly 20 x 1e9 = 20B tokens, so 100B is already 5x over, which is sensible for a small model that will be served cheaply (see the scaling-laws chunk).
  6. Fix / recommendation: Propose the cheaper path first: continue pretraining (or SFT) an open 1B-class model on the domain data with a replay mix of general data to limit forgetting; use from-scratch only if license, vocabulary or data-privacy reasons demand it. Reserve 8 GPUs, plan for ~1 week with checkpointing and an eval harness; the dominant costs are data prep and evaluation, not GPUs.
  7. Prevention: Written requirement doc: target metric, baseline, budget, stop criteria; loss and eval tracking; checkpoints every N steps.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't promise quality from a compute number, and I wouldn't train from scratch before seeing the baseline's score.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• They then say 7B instead of 1B. → 6 x 7e9 x 1e11 = 4.2e21 FLOPs -> ~2,950 GPU-hours at 40% MFU: ~46 hours on 64 GPUs; needs multi-node parallelism, the engineering jumps.
  • MFU turns out 15%. → Time grows 2.7x; profile data loading and communication.
  • Could you use fewer tokens? → Yes, but below ~20 tokens/parameter you leave compute-optimal territory; repeated epochs have diminishing returns.

sections.label: Senior war story
