sections.html: A "train our own model" request turned into a 3-day continued pretraining job on an open checkpoint, which beat the from-scratch pilot on the domain eval at a fraction of cost; the pilot's value was proving the data pipeline.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Guesses or accepts the premise.
  • Hire: Computes 6ND and GPU-hours with MFU, asks about alternatives.
  • Strong hire: Challenges from-scratch, ties tokens to Chinchilla ratio, plans a pilot and replay mix.

questions.contextHtml: Post-incident review. A team serving an 8B bf16 model (16 GB weights, 32 layers, 8 KV heads, d_head 128 -> 128 KiB KV/token) on one H100 80 GB (HBM ~3.35 TB/s; verify) raised the engine's max concurrent sequences from 64 to 256, expecting ~4x throughput. Traffic: ~4,000-token contexts. Results: throughput rose only 16%, inter-token latency p99 went from 15 ms to 23 ms (SLO 20 ms), and the engine logged preemptions ("sequence preempted: KV cache full"). Nobody changed the model or kernels. GPU utilization (as shown by nvidia-smi) was already "98%" before the change.
questions.promptHtml: Explain why 4x batch gave ~1.16x throughput and recommend the setting.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The GPU was already saturated, so nothing helps." This confuses "busy" with compute-saturated and doesn't compute KV memory or bytes read per step.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the KV capacity the engine reports? Are preemptions recompute or swap? What's the average context? Does the batch include prefills? Which attention kernel?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back to 64-100 concurrent sequences to restore the ITL SLO.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) KV cache capacity caps real concurrency at ~110; the extra sequences are preempted and recomputed, wasting work. (b) Per-step bytes grow with batch because KV reads scale with sequences, so there's no free amortization of weights. (c) Compute saturation (unlikely at this arithmetic intensity). (d) Scheduler overhead.
  4. How I'd verify each: Engine metrics (KV cache usage, running vs waiting vs preempted); roofline estimate; profile with Nsight or the engine profiler to see time in attention vs GEMMs.
  5. Root cause (the math):
    • KV per 4,000-token sequence: 4,000 x 128 KiB = 500 MiB = 0.49 GiB.
    • HBM budget: 80 GB x 0.9 = 72 GB minus 16 GB weights = ~56 GB -> about 110 sequences max.
    • Decode step time is approximately (weight bytes + KV bytes read) / bandwidth.
      • Batch 64: 16.1 GB + 64 x 0.524 GB (=33.5 GB) = 49.6 GB / 3.35 TB/s = 14.8 ms -> 64 / 0.0148 = 4,300 tokens/s.
      • Batch ~110 (capacity): 16.1 + 57.7 = 73.8 GB -> 22 ms -> 5,000 tokens/s (+16%).
    • Weights are amortized across the batch but KV reads are per-sequence, so once KV bytes rival weight bytes, extra batch buys little throughput and increases latency. The other 146 requested sequences cannot fit and are preempted.
    • Arithmetic intensity per decode step at batch 110: FLOPs = 2 x 8e9 x 110 = 1.76e12 vs 74 GB read: 24 FLOPs/byte, far below H100's ridge point (~989e12 / 3.35e12 = 295 FLOPs/byte). Still bandwidth-bound; nvidia-smi "utilization" only means a kernel was running.
  6. Fix: Set max sequences to ~64-96 for the ITL SLO; enable fp8 KV (halves KV bytes; evaluate quality) or quantized weights to raise efficiency; use GQA models only; scale out with more replicas rather than bigger batches; use speculative decoding (serving chunk) for latency.
  7. Prevention: Capacity formula in runbook; SLO-driven (not max-throughput) tuning; alert on preemption count > 0; load test sweeps of concurrency vs ITL to find the knee.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't chase GPU-util %; I wouldn't set concurrency above KV capacity; I wouldn't claim throughput is the only objective: latency SLO decides.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if contexts were 500 tokens? → KV is 8x smaller (0.06 GiB), capacity ~900 sequences, weights dominate bytes, so batching 256 would give a large throughput gain until compute binds around batch of a few hundred.
  • Why not just add a second GPU for the same replica? → TP shards both weights and KV (more HBM, more bandwidth) but adds all-reduce latency; at 8B a second replica is typically better.
  • Does MQA/GQA change this? → KV bytes per sequence shrink, moving the knee to a higher batch; that's why GQA models batch better.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A throughput tuning sprint "found" a 4x config in a short-context benchmark; production's long contexts moved the knee from 256 to 70 sequences. The benchmark's context distribution was the bug.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Says GPU is saturated.
  • Hire: Computes KV capacity and recognizes per-sequence KV reads.
  • Strong hire: Full step-time model, roofline ridge comparison, SLO-driven recommendation, and benchmark-context caveat.

questions.contextHtml:
You are writing a custom inference runtime that loads Hugging Face-format Llama weights. Short prompts (<100 tokens) look fine, but on 2k-token documents answers degrade: perplexity on a 2k-token eval is 7.9 versus the reference 5.1 (same weights, same tokenizer), and greedy outputs diverge from the reference after about 30 tokens. Your RoPE code:

def rope_interleaved(x, pos, base=10000.0):
    # x: [B, h, T, dk]; pos: [T]
    dk = x.shape[-1]
    inv = base ** (-torch.arange(0, dk, 2).float() / dk)     # [dk/2]
    ang = pos[:, None].float() * inv[None, :]                # [T, dk/2]
    cos, sin = ang.cos(), ang.sin()
    x_even, x_odd = x[..., 0::2], x[..., 1::2]               # adjacent pairs
    out = torch.empty_like(x)
    out[..., 0::2] = x_even * cos - x_odd * sin
    out[..., 1::2] = x_even * sin + x_odd * cos
    return out

The config says rope_theta = 500000.0. Weight files come from LlamaForCausalLM safetensors.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, why do short prompts hide it, and how do you prove and fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Maybe numerical precision" or "long context needs scaling." Doesn't notice the config theta isn't used or the pairing convention.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which checkpoint format (original Meta or HF)? Was rope_theta read from config? Does the reference apply rope_scaling? Which dtype? Are position ids correct in decode?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Fall back to the reference implementation for the affected deployment; do not ship the custom runtime.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Pairing convention mismatch: HF Llama uses the half-split rotate_half layout (dim i paired with i + dk/2), while this code pairs adjacent dims. (b) Wrong base: hardcoded 10000 vs configured 500000. (c) Missing rope_scaling for models that define it. (d) Position ids reset in decode.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare the post-RoPE Q/K tensors with the reference layer by layer on a single prompt (max abs diff); swap in rotate_half and re-measure; test with base 500000; run a relative-position invariance test (shift all positions by k, attention scores should be unchanged).
  5. Root cause: The HF conversion script permutes Q and K rows from Meta's interleaved layout into the half-split layout, so applying an interleaved rotation to HF weights rotates the wrong pairs of dimensions. Dimensions are rotated with the frequency belonging to a different pair, so the dot product no longer depends only on relative position. At short range the angles are small for the low-frequency pairs but high-frequency pairs mismatch immediately; short prompts hide it because the model leans on local, high-frequency structure that is more forgiving, and errors compound with distance. The hardcoded base of 10000 additionally uses wrong frequencies: with 500000 the wavelengths are much longer.
  6. Fix:
def rope_hf(x, pos, base):                      # half-split, matches HF Llama
    dk = x.shape[-1]; half = dk // 2
    inv = base ** (-torch.arange(0, half).float() / half)
    ang = pos[:, None].float() * inv[None, :]
    cos = torch.cat([ang.cos(), ang.cos()], -1)
    sin = torch.cat([ang.sin(), ang.sin()], -1)
    x1, x2 = x[..., :half], x[..., half:]
    rot = torch.cat([-x2, x1], -1)               # rotate_half
    return x * cos + rot * sin

Read rope_theta and rope_scaling from config. 7. Prevention: Golden-output tests against the reference implementation for every supported model (layer outputs and logits), shift-invariance test, config-driven RoPE. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't permute weights at load unless I own the conversion and keep a test; I wouldn't call it a "precision issue" without diffing tensors.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Both layouts give the same math? → Yes if weights match the layout; the layouts are a permutation of dimensions; mixing them breaks equivalence.
  • Where else do convention bugs hide? → Cached keys stored pre- vs post-rotation, position ids in batched left-padded decode, and rope_scaling factors.
  • Why does shift invariance test work? → RoPE makes scores depend only on position difference; a mismatched pairing breaks that property.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A port to a new accelerator matched logits for 20 tokens and drifted afterwards. Per-layer tensor diffs located it in the first attention layer in an hour; the team added golden tests for every config thereafter.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blames precision or context length.
  • Hire: Finds pairing/layout mismatch or base mismatch and compares tensors to a reference.
  • Strong hire: Finds both, explains why short prompts hide it, adds golden and shift-invariance tests.

questions.promptHtml: What have we learned about what attention heads actually do? Explain induction heads and attention sinks, and why they matter in practice.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who know mechanistic findings relevant to in-context learning and long-context serving from those who only know the formula.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Induction heads are a two-head circuit that finds an earlier occurrence of the current token and copies what came next, which is a main mechanism behind in-context pattern completion. Attention sinks are tokens, usually the first, that soak up a large share of attention mass because softmax must sum to one; keeping them in the cache is what makes sliding-window streaming work. Both are empirical findings, not guarantees."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Induction heads (Olsson et al., Anthropic, 2022): Pattern [A][B] ... [A] -> predict [B]. A previous-token head in an earlier layer writes "my previous token was A" into the residual stream at position of B; a later induction head at the second [A] queries for positions whose "previous token = A" and attends to B, copying B's identity to the output. The paper links their formation to an abrupt "phase change" in training loss and in-context learning ability (correlational evidence at small scale, argued for larger; verify specifics). Practical relevance: few-shot prompting, copying of names and code identifiers, and why repetition loops are easy to fall into.

Attention sinks (Xiao et al., StreamingLLM, 2023): softmax forces attention weights to sum to 1, so when no key is relevant the head must put the mass somewhere. Models learn to park it on the first token(s), whose values are near zero-effect. If you evict those tokens in a sliding-window cache, outputs degrade sharply (perplexity blows up); keeping a few initial "sink" tokens plus a recent window restores stable generation without fine-tuning. This is cache-eviction guidance, and explains why naive sliding-window truncation of the start of a conversation can break a model that was not trained with a window. Related: "massive activations" in a few residual dimensions at those tokens.

Other observed head types: previous-token heads, positional heads, name-mover heads. Many heads are redundant and prunable; interpretability claims are circuit-level for small/mid models and weaker at frontier scale.

Practical takeaways: don't assume "attention weight = importance/explanation" (attention weights are not faithful explanations); position of important info and sink behavior influence long-context design; gpt-oss style models add learned sink logits (verify) in architecture to address this.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
# Streaming cache policy sketch: keep first n_sink tokens + last n_recent
def evict(kv, n_sink=4, n_recent=1020):
    if kv.shape[2] <= n_sink + n_recent:
        return kv
    return torch.cat([kv[:, :, :n_sink], kv[:, :, -n_recent:]], dim=2)

(With RoPE, remember to use cache-relative positions per the StreamingLLM approach; verify implementation details.)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating attention maps as explanations of model decisions.
  • Believing the first token is attended to because of its content; it is a structural dump.
  • Evicting the oldest tokens including sinks in a rolling cache.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does StreamingLLM give long-term memory? → No; it keeps stable generation over long streams but forgets evicted content.
  2. How do induction heads relate to in-context learning? → Strong correlation in training dynamics; they implement fuzzy copy/complete; they aren't the whole story.
  3. Why do softmax sinks exist? → Normalization needs an outlet when there's no good match; a learnable sink logit or softmax-off-by-one variants address this.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "heads learn different things." Senior: names the circuits, the training-dynamics evidence, the sink phenomenon, and the practical cache-eviction consequence.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A chat product truncated old turns by dropping the oldest tokens from a rolling KV window and saw sudden gibberish after the window filled; keeping the first few tokens (or recomputing prefill from a clean truncation) fixed it.

questions.contextHtml:
You are asked to design a ~1.2B parameter decoder for on-device assistant use (phone, 4 GB memory budget for the model plus cache, 4-bit weights ~0.6 GB at 1.2B params, bf16/fp16 or int8 KV cache, contexts up to 8k, tokens/s matters on a memory-bandwidth-limited phone SoC). Vocabulary 128k. Two candidate shapes with ~equal parameter counts:

  • A: d = 2048, L = 16, 32 heads, 8 KV heads, d_head 64, SwiGLU d_ff = 8192, tied embeddings.
  • B: d = 1536, L = 28, 24 heads, 8 KV heads, d_head 64, d_ff = 6144, tied embeddings. Product wants strong reasoning-ish quality, low latency, and small cache.
questions.promptHtml: Compare A and B on params, KV cache, latency and likely quality, and pick one.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Deeper is better" or "wider is faster" with no numbers, ignoring the embedding share and KV math.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which tasks and evals decide quality? Is the target hardware batch-1? Is training compute fixed? Can we distill from a bigger teacher? Which runtime/kernels (head-dim support)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A (design). I'd first verify param counts.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) KV cache and per-token latency favor fewer layers. (b) Quality per parameter favors some depth, within limits. (c) The 128k vocabulary eats a big share of parameters at small scale. (d) Distillation and data quality matter more than the shape.
  4. How I'd verify each: Param calculator; small-scale sweeps (e.g. 100M-scale proxies) at equal tokens; measure tokens/s on the target runtime; eval on the target tasks.
  5. Root cause (the math):
    • A per layer: attention Q 2048 x 2048 = 4.19M, O 4.19M, K and V each 2048 x 512 = 1.05M -> 10.5M; FFN 3 x 2048 x 8192 = 50.3M; layer 60.8M x 16 = 973M; embedding 128,256 x 2048 = 262.7M (tied) -> 1.236B.
    • B per layer: Q 1536 x 1536 = 2.36M, O 2.36M, K and V 1536 x 512 = 0.79M each -> 6.29M; FFN 3 x 1536 x 6144 = 28.3M; layer 34.6M x 28 = 969M; embedding 197M -> 1.166B.
    • KV per token: A = 2 x 16 x 8 x 64 x 2 B = 32 KiB; B = 2 x 28 x 8 x 64 x 2 B = 56 KiB. At 8k context: A = 256 MiB, B = 448 MiB.
    • Decode speed is bandwidth-bound: bytes per token read = weights (~0.6 GB at 4-bit for both) + KV; both similar, but B has 75% more layers, i.e. more sequential kernel launches and smaller matmuls with worse utilization on small hardware.
    • Embedding share: A 21%, B 17%. Depth generally improves reasoning/compositional ability for a given parameter count up to a point (for small models, deeper-thinner has been reported to help; MobileLLM reported this for sub-billion models, verify), but cost is latency and cache.
  6. Fix / recommendation: I'd pick A for latency and cache simplicity if eval gap on pilot runs is within noise; pick B if the pilot shows a clear reasoning gain worth ~15-30% lower tokens/s (measure). Use distillation from a larger teacher and tied embeddings; consider fp8/int8 KV to halve cache.
  7. Prevention: Decision doc with measured numbers; keep configuration parameterized so the sweep can be rerun when hardware changes.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't pick shape from intuition alone; and I wouldn't increase vocab for multilingual without accounting for embedding cost; I wouldn't untie embeddings at this size without evidence.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Marketing wants 32k context. → A's cache = 1 GiB, B's = 1.75 GiB at 16-bit: over budget with weights; need KV quantization, sliding-window layers or a smaller KV head count.
  • What if the NPU only supports head dim 64/128 kernels? → Both qualify; check kernel support first.
  • What about MoE for small models? → Increases memory footprint for little active-compute gain on-device; usually not worth it here.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team picked a "deep-thin" shape from a paper; on the phone runtime the extra layers' kernel-launch overhead wiped out the theoretical win, which was only visible when benchmarked on device.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Chooses by intuition.
  • Hire: Computes params and KV for both and explains the bandwidth-bound decode.
  • Strong hire: Includes embedding share, device-kernel effects, pilot sweeps, and distillation.

questions.promptHtml: Beyond GQA, what techniques cut attention's cost or KV memory at long context (sliding-window, local/global layers, MLA), and what do they trade away?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Long context is the frontier of architecture work; seniors should place techniques on a compute/memory/quality map.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Sliding-window attention limits each token to a fixed recent window so cache and compute become O(window); information still propagates across layers, but exact long-range recall is limited. Interleaving local and global layers keeps a few full-context layers. Multi-head latent attention compresses K and V into a low-rank latent per token so the cache is much smaller while keeping near-MHA quality. Each trades exactness or complexity for memory."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Sliding-window attention (SWA): token i attends to i-W..i. Cost per token O(W), cache capped at W per layer (a rolling buffer). Because layers stack, the effective receptive field grows as L x W (Mistral 7B used W = 4,096 with 32 layers; verify), but information passes through lossy hops, so precise retrieval from beyond W is poor. Local/global interleaving (e.g. several local layers per global layer in some recent models; verify per model) restores access to the full context at a fraction of the cost: KV cache is dominated by the global layers.

MLA (DeepSeek-V2): instead of caching K and V per head, project the hidden state to a low-dimensional latent c (e.g. a few hundred dims) and cache c (plus a small decoupled RoPE key); K and V are reconstructed by up-projections, which can be absorbed into the Q and output projections at inference, so you never materialize full K/V. The paper reports a large KV cache reduction versus MHA (verify the numbers in the paper). Cost: more complicated kernels and RoPE handling (RoPE can't simply be applied after up-projection, hence the decoupled part).

Others: sparse patterns (Longformer, BigBird: local + global tokens + random), linear attention/state-space hybrids (constant-size state; recall weaker; see the architectures chunk), KV cache compression/eviction (H2O, SnapKV style; lossy; verify), KV quantization (fp8/int8/int4).

technique          compute     KV memory    exact long-range?
full MHA           O(n^2)      n*L*h*dk     yes
GQA                O(n^2)      n*L*g*dk     yes
SWA (window W)     O(n*W)      W*L*g*dk     no (indirect via depth)
local+global mix   mixed       mostly global layers   yes in global layers
MLA                O(n^2)      n*L*(latent) yes

Key distinction: GQA/MLA/KV-quantization reduce memory and bandwidth but keep full attention (O(n^2) compute); SWA/sparse reduce both but forfeit exact recall.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying sliding window "supports" long context equivalent to full attention.
  • Applying a sliding window at inference to a model trained with full attention (breaks sinks; see the attention-sinks question).
  • Assuming FlashAttention changes the asymptotic compute.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How does an SWA rolling buffer work? → Position i writes to slot i mod W; older entries are overwritten.
  2. Why can't MLA just apply RoPE to the up-projected keys? → RoPE is position dependent and wouldn't commute with absorbing up-projections into the query side, so a small separate RoPE component is cached.
  3. Which technique would you use for 128k with a fixed memory budget? → Combine GQA/MLA, KV quantization, and local/global layers, then evaluate retrieval at the target length.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: names SWA. Senior: maps each technique onto compute vs memory vs recall, explains MLA's RoPE complication, and warns about train/inference mismatch.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team enabled aggressive KV eviction to fit 100k contexts and passed perplexity checks yet failed needle-style retrieval; evaluation must test recall, not just fluency.

questions.contextHtml: A 3B-parameter model is being continued-pretrained in fp16 mixed precision (loss scaling on) on 64 GPUs after a data-mix change. At step 41,200 the loss jumps from 2.31 to 9.8 and the log shows grad_norm: inf for 12 consecutive steps, then training reports nan loss. The same config was stable in bf16 on a previous run. Logs show attention logits in layer 24 with max |score| ~ 7.3e4 (pre-softmax) shortly before the failure. Data team notes the new mix contains many long repetitive log files. The infra team suspects a bad node.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix. What's the mechanism, and how do you avoid a restart loop?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Lower the learning rate and restart from the last checkpoint," without identifying the overflow mechanism, or blaming hardware without evidence.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is softmax computed in fp32? Does the kernel accumulate in fp32? Do we have QK-norm or logit soft-capping? Is the NaN reproducible on the same batch on a different node? When was the last good checkpoint, and which data shard was in flight?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Halt the run; roll back to the last good checkpoint before the spike; skip the offending data shard; reduce LR for a window if needed.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Attention logits exceeding fp16's max (65,504) overflow to inf, producing inf/NaN in softmax. (b) Loss-scaling overflow cascade. (c) A bad batch (long repetitive sequences cause very peaked attention and growing Q/K norms). (d) Hardware fault. Node issues would show on a single rank rather than globally.
  4. How I'd verify each: Replay the failing batch from the checkpoint on another node (deterministic repro); log per-layer max attention logit and Q/K norms; check the grad-norm trend before the incident; compare fp32 vs fp16 forward on the batch.
  5. Root cause: Max |score| 7.3e4 > 65,504, so q.k in fp16 overflowed to inf; softmax(inf, ...) gives NaN, loss scaling reduced the scale repeatedly but the forward itself was already non-finite. Repetitive inputs encourage large Q/K norms (the model sharpens attention onto repeated patterns), pushing logits up; the sqrt(d_k) scale only controls variance at initialization.
  6. Fix: Short term: roll back and skip the shard; switch to bf16 (8-bit exponent, same range as fp32; cost: fewer mantissa bits) if hardware supports it; ensure the attention kernel computes scores/softmax in fp32 (fused kernels such as FlashAttention do softmax accumulation in fp32). Long term: add QK-norm (normalize Q and K per head before the dot product) or logit soft-capping, lower the Adam beta2 / add z-loss-style regularization on logits, gradient clipping at 1.0, data filtering of degenerate repetitive documents.
  7. Prevention: Monitor max attention logit and Q/K norms per layer; alert at 50% of dtype max; automatic skip-and-resume on non-finite grads with batch logging; canary evals of new data mixes with short runs.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't just lower LR and resume (it hides an overflow); I wouldn't swap hardware before a deterministic repro; QK-norm changes the model (it needs training from early on or careful adaptation, not a drop-in at step 41k).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why is bf16 safer? → Same exponent range as fp32 (max ~3.4e38), so overflow is rare; the trade-off is precision, which matters for accumulations kept in fp32.
  • Why not just clip the logits? → Clipping or soft-capping (tanh scaling) is a model change; if done at inference only it shifts behavior.
  • Does inference in fp16 face the same risk? → Yes for models with large activations; many checkpoints are released in bf16 and fp16 serving can overflow, check for inf in logits.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A run diverged twice at different steps; both times the batch came from the same scraped-logs source. Down-weighting that source and adding per-layer logit monitors made the third attempt boring.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Lower LR and restart, or blames hardware.
  • Hire: Identifies fp16 overflow in attention logits and proposes bf16/fp32 softmax.
  • Strong hire: Repro on another node, QK-norm and monitoring, data-mix root cause, and rollback/skip procedure.

questions.contextHtml: You serve a 128,256-vocabulary model (d = 4096) via a Hugging Face-based endpoint on a 24 GB GPU. Short prompts are fine. For 8,192-token prompts the process OOMs during prefill even though the KV cache for one sequence is only ~1 GiB (128 KiB/token) and weights are ~15 GiB (the logs show CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 3.91 GiB). Memory profile shows a single large allocation right at the end of the forward pass. A teammate proposes upgrading to a 48 GB GPU. Another proposes lowering max context to 4k.
questions.promptHtml: Find the cause and a cheaper fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Accepts the GPU upgrade or the context cut. Doesn't connect the 3.91 GiB to vocab x tokens.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are logits computed for all positions? Which dtype is the output cast to? Which library and version (does it support computing only last-position logits)? Batch size at prefill?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap prompt length or prefill chunk size to stay under memory; restart with a lower batch.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Full-sequence logits tensor [T, V] materialized in fp32. (b) Attention score materialization (naive kernel). (c) Fragmentation. (d) KV overflow (ruled out by the math).
  4. How I'd verify each: Compute: 8,192 x 128,256 x 4 B = 4.2e9 B = 3.91 GiB, which matches the failing allocation exactly. Check with torch.cuda.memory_summary() and by printing logits shape.
  5. Root cause: The LM head projects every position's hidden state [8192, 4096] to vocabulary logits [8192, 128256]; with an fp32 upcast that's 3.91 GiB (bf16 would be 1.96 GiB), plus a softmax/copy of the same size. For generation, only the last position's logits are needed (128,256 x 4 B = 0.5 MB). Large vocab models make this tensor huge; batch of 4 prompts would need 15.6 GiB.
  6. Fix: Compute logits only for the final position at prefill (recent transformers versions expose logits_to_keep / earlier num_logits_to_keep; verify your version) or use a serving engine (vLLM, TGI) that already slices hidden states before the head. For scoring/perplexity use chunked cross-entropy (compute loss in chunks of ~1k tokens). Avoid the fp32 upcast when not needed.
out = model(input_ids, logits_to_keep=1)   # logits shape [B, 1, V]; verify arg name for your version
next_logits = out.logits[:, -1]
  1. Prevention: Memory model in the capacity doc: weights + KV + logits (T x V x bytes) + activations; load test with the max prompt length, not the median; alert on peak allocation vs total.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't buy a bigger GPU for a bug that costs 4 GiB, or cut context and degrade product features. Tied embeddings and vocabulary size are model design choices, not something to change at serving time.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why did short prompts work? → The logits tensor scales linearly with T: 512 tokens = 0.24 GiB.
  • Does the same problem affect training? → Yes: loss over all positions needs logits [B x T, V]; fused/chunked cross-entropy kernels avoid materializing it.
  • Does vocabulary size also affect speed? → The head matmul costs 2 x d x V = 1.05 GFLOPs per token at decode, about 6% of 2N for an 8B model; sampling/softmax over 128k entries adds small overhead.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A scoring service OOMed only on long documents; the culprit was logits for every token when only five answer tokens mattered. Slicing the hidden states first cut peak memory by 4 GiB and removed the need for a GPU upgrade.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Upgrades GPU or shortens context.
  • Hire: Computes T x V x 4 B and matches the allocation, slices to the last position.
  • Strong hire: Notes training-time chunked loss, engine behavior, memory model for capacity docs, and the decode-time head cost.
